## A biomarker that changes its mind

::: columns
::: {.column width="36%"}
In a late-stage oncology trial, one biomarker looked **unrelated to survival**.

One Cox coefficient **≈ 0**.

::: {.fragment fragment-index=1 style="margin-top:.5em;"}
The curve is **orthoMTL**: one estimate per landmark.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="64%"}
::: {.fragment fragment-index=1}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 7.0
#| fig-height: 4.3
#| out-width: "100%"
sign_flip_fig()
```
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2 style="text-align:center; font-size:1.0em; margin-top:-.5em;"}
**Harmful early. Protective late.** The two halves cancelled out.
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=3 style="text-align:center; font-size:.9em; margin-top:.1em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
So how does orthoMTL get one estimate per landmark?
:::

::: notes
SAY FIRST, before the curve - this is the bridge from the title, and the only
place the agent is named before slide 3: "Our package found an effect that flips
sign halfway through a cancer trial. Then I spent six weeks fighting a LICENSE
field - and most of that work was done by an AI agent. This talk is whether the
agent needed my instructions to do it."

SAY: the slide opens with TEXT ONLY, no figure - set up the puzzle first ("one
coefficient, essentially zero, so the biomarker looks like nothing"). Click 1
brings up the orthoMTL line AND the curve together: "below zero is worse
survival." Click 2 for the hook, pause after "the two halves cancelled out".
Click 3 is the orange question - walk straight into slide 3, do not add a
second transition.

DON'T: name any compound, gene, trial or variable. The figure is a redrawn
schematic, captioned as illustrative - it shows the KIND of output orthoMTL
gives, it is not a screenshot of a package run. Say "this is the shape orthoMTL
recovers", never "here is our output". Do NOT say the landmark estimates are
null - they are not. The ~0 is the single proportional-hazards coefficient
over all follow-up; the curve beside it is what you see after splitting.

IF ASKED "so the effect is significant at the landmarks?": yes, that is the
point - one average coefficient hides it, landmark-wise estimates do not.

IF ASKED which biomarker: "I can't name it here; the published analysis is in the
reference on the last slide."
:::

## orthoMTL: don't average over time

::: columns
::: {.column width="38%"}
Cut follow-up into **landmarks**: one yes/no task each.

Fit them **together**, each with **its own effect**.
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 6.6
#| fig-height: 3.9
#| out-width: "100%"
landmark_fig()
```

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393; text-align:center; margin-top:-.2em;"}
Framing after MTLSA (Li et al., KDD 2016).
:::
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.25em; margin-top:.3em;"}
**`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`** (on CRAN, 2026)
:::

::: notes
SAY: "If your outcome is time-to-event and you suspect effects change over time,
this package shows you that." Click for the link. 35 seconds, no more.

IF ASKED "isn't this just non-proportional hazards - why not coxph with tt(), landmark
Cox or RMST?": those are right for a handful of covariates with an assumed shape.
[VERIFY BEFORE USE - draft] orthoMTL is for many candidate features: landmark tasks
are fitted jointly with a penalty, effects can differ between landmarks with no
parametric time function, and tasks borrow strength where the data agree.
Refs: Vervier 2014 (method), Juric 2026 Annals of Oncology (application).
:::

## From PhD code to CRAN

Twelve-year-old research code. 

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
An **AI agent**, a language model that edits files
and runs commands itself, did the packaging, **in a chat, with me in the loop**.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
Writing unit tests for the **logistic loss**, it found a **real bug** in my own 2014
gradient: labels were ±1, the code used the 0/1 formula. I checked it by hand.
It was real and fixed.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.7em; font-size:1.15em;"}
Then every automated check went green:

::: {style="text-align:center; font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.2em;"}
`R CMD check`: **0 errors | 0 warnings**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.05em; margin-top:.5em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Tests pass. Checks pass. Bundle built. Submit.
:::

::: notes
SAY: the story, plainly, then land the green check. Beat on "Submit." - the
audience should believe this is the happy ending. Slide 5 breaks it.

STRESS "with me in the loop": this was interactive, a chat, back and forth,
me answering its questions. That is the contrast the result slide pays off -
the 57 runs had nobody to ask.

The bug: found while writing unit tests for the logistic loss, I verified by
hand, the code was fixed. The test was the symmetry check - flip every label,
the answer must flip. It didn't.

DON'T: claim the agent "understood" the maths, and do NOT claim I designed the
test - the agent wrote it. Precision on the check: it was 0 errors, 0 warnings
and 1 NOTE ("New submission"), which is normal and expected for a first
submission. Say "no errors, no warnings" - if anyone asks about the note, that
is what it was.

IF ASKED for the test: fit on y, fit on -y, predictions must be 1 - p. Full
sketch is on the correctness backup slide.
:::

## Then CRAN rejected us. Twice. {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.5em; line-height:1.9; margin-top:.5em;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** An invalid `LICENSE` field.
:::
::: {.fragment}
**2.** A hard-coded `set.seed()`.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.7em; color:#FF4E00;"}
No automated check caught either. **A CRAN volunteer** caught both.
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.6em;"}
Both were **knowledge the agent didn't have**. I could have written it down and
handed it over.
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.05em; margin-top:.4em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
People call that a **skill file**.
:::

::: notes
SAY: open by puncturing the previous slide - "so we submitted, and it came
back. Twice." Then slow, big pauses. "Each one cost weeks of round-trips - and
the people who caught them are volunteers."

Then the turn, in your own words: neither rejection was a coding failure. Both
were things the agent simply did not know. That is fixable by writing it down -
and that is what a skill file is. Land the orange line and go straight to
slide 6, which defines it.

DON'T: say the skill file would have worked. The whole talk is that question
being open. Here you are only naming the idea.

IF ASKED: the CRAN Repository Policy's own preamble says CRAN is maintained by
volunteers and calls their time its most precious resource.
:::

## What is a skill file?

::: columns
::: {.column width="40%"}
A **Markdown file of instructions** the agent reads before it starts.

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.8em; font-weight:700;"}
Would one have got us through CRAN in one shot?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {style="margin-top:1.6em;"}
```markdown
# CRAN submission notes for this package

## 1. Do not set a seed to a specific number
##    inside a function
- Search every file in `R/` for `set.seed(`.
- Give the function a `seed = NULL` argument ...
```

::: {style="font-size:.5em; color:#939393;"}
Excerpt (abridged): the file I later wrote from our own two rejections.
:::
:::
:::
:::

::: notes
SAY: answer the question slide 5 just raised - "it is nothing exotic. It is a
Markdown file the agent reads before it starts." Posit and others publish CRAN
ones, people drop them into their projects. Click: the question. 30 seconds.

IF ASKED: in this study the file was always loaded (as CLAUDE.md), not fetched on
demand by a Skill tool.
:::

```{r}
design_fig(2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| fig-width: 12

#| out-width: "100%"
design_fig(3)
```
:::
:::

::: notes
SAY, one breath per click: "Same starting package every time." Click: "Five arms,
block-randomised." Click: "Scored blind. We expected the machine check to floor, so
the AI judge was the primary measure." Do not read the boxes aloud.

Click the last line and STRESS it, pointing at the "One agent, no human" box:
the packaging you saw on slide 4 was a conversation. These 57 runs were not.
One frozen prompt in, headless, nobody present to answer a single question.
Sets up the result.

CHECKPOINT: leave this slide by 4:00.

DON'T: say "nobody measures skill files" - skills are measured; the point is the
measurements are already conditional.

IF ASKED "isn't giving every arm the CRAN docs stacking the deck against the
skill files?" - this is the most likely challenge in the room, and the answer
is a trial analogy. Every arm gets the standard of care (the official CRAN
documentation at a known path); the arms differ only in whether a skill file is
added on top. It is an ADD-ON trial against an ACTIVE control, not placebo. The
question is not "does an agent need CRAN knowledge" - obviously it does - but
"does a distilled skill file add anything on top of the documentation already
being there". That is the question a maintainer actually faces.

Say it was pre-specified, because it was: the preregistration says a skill
effect measured against a handbook-equipped control is a CONSERVATIVE estimate,
and that handicapping the control by withholding the handbook would produce a
larger effect and an indefensible one. The choice biases AGAINST my own
hypothesis, and I made it before unblinding.

CONCEDE, in my own words, before anyone digs: this makes the control stronger
than my original packaging run was. I only referred to the CRAN docs partly -
and to be straight about it, what the agent had access to was never a
consideration back then. That first pass was me trying agentic AI on my own
package, not running a protocol, so there was no design decision to record and
nothing to measure. The controlled version is the experiment; the first pass
was the thing that made me want one. So this is not a replay of our submission:
it tests a more favourable baseline on purpose. External validity, not a flaw.

DON'T dress the first pass up as an uncontrolled arm or say the trace is
"lost". There was no protocol, so there was nothing to lose. Equally, do not
claim the original agent did or did not read the docs - I cannot say, and CRAN
rules may well be in the model's training data anyway.
IF ASKED about the literature: SkillDelta and SkillAxe report skills "often provide
no benefit". SkillsBench finds +16.6 pp, but on 87 tasks admitted only if
"significantly easier with Skills", top-quartile skills, and none in R; its
software-engineering domain gains second-least of eight. Backup has the detail.
IF ASKED why the control has n = 20: the protocol deviation, "not claiming" slide.
IF ASKED which skills: posit-dev/skills (cran-extrachecks, r-package-development),
CoryMcCartan/agent-skills (cran-submit); backup arms table.
:::

## The result {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="text-align:center; margin-top:.1em;"}
::: {style="font-size:5em; font-weight:700; color:#FF4E00; line-height:1;"}
`r n_seed`/`r n_runs`
:::
::: {style="font-size:1.3em; margin-top:.2em;"}
runs fixed all four planted defects, **control included**
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.1em; margin-top:.6em;"}
`R CMD check` clean in **`r n_runs`/`r n_runs`**. Submission-ready, with
**no human in the loop at all**.
:::

::: {.fragment style="text-align:center; font-size:1.05em; margin-top:.5em;"}
The agent did just as well with **no skill file at all**.
:::

::: notes
SAY: let the number sit for two seconds. "Including the control - all twenty runs."

Click 1 is the one to sell, and it is NOT a skill-file point: every one of the
57 runs came back clean under R CMD check, starting from a deliberately broken
package, with one prompt and nobody to ask. The packaging on slide 4 was a
conversation; this was not. "Zero interaction, submission-ready."

Click 2, then say the ceiling line OUT LOUD - it is no longer on the slide,
and it has to be you who says it, before anyone in the room does: "that is a
ceiling, and I'll say it before you do." Everything landed at the top, so
there was no room for a skill file to show a difference.

DON'T overclaim "ready to publish": R CMD check clean is NOT the same as CRAN
accepting it - this whole talk is that gap, and our own set.seed rejection
passed a clean check. Say "clean under R CMD check", never "CRAN would have
taken it". Also do not say zero notes: the New submission note is normal.

IF ASKED about the LICENSE defect (the one planted defect R CMD check does not report):
fixed in every run, every arm, control included.
IF ASKED "models keep improving - isn't this moot?": that cuts my way; a better model
needs the checklist less.
IF ASKED "then why write CRAN skill files?": most were written for weaker models;
they encode what the check can't see (two slides on); and nobody had measured it.
:::

## Why the control did so well

::: {style="font-size:1.2em; margin-top:.6em;"}
::: {.fragment}
The agent runs **`R CMD check`** and reads its own failures.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em;"}
A machine check beats a checklist: it reads **your** package, not a generic one.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Skill files add little where a tool already tells the truth.
:::
:::

::: notes
SAY: three clicks, one line each. Then the bridge: "So a skill file can only help
where the check is silent."

IF ASKED, the other half of why the check wins (deliberately off the slide, it
was one word too many): a written checklist also reflects whenever its author
last updated it, while the check enforces the rules as they currently stand.

DON'T: frame this as against skill files - it is about where they pay.

IF ASKED: SkillFlow found agents used retrieved skills 70% of the time and still
gained nothing. Reading a skill is not the same as needing one.
:::

## Where the check is silent: `set.seed()`

::: columns
::: {.column width="48%"}
`set.seed(42)` inside four exported functions: our second rejection.

`R CMD check` says nothing.

Here, the arms **did** differ.

::: {style="margin-top:.8em; color:#939393; font-size:.8em;"}
Post-hoc, exploratory.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="52%"}
| Arm | `seed = NULL` fix |
|:--|--:|
| Control | **0** / 20 |
| Checklist | 0 / 9 |
| Process | **7** / 9 |
| General R | 0 / 10 |
| Handbook | **8** / 9 |
:::
:::

::: notes
SAY: "The one rejection the tool can't see - and here the arms differ."

The slide only says "post-hoc, exploratory", so SAY THE REST OUT LOUD: this
check was run after unblinding, on one criterion, with no test. "A lead, not a
result." Then, in the same breath, the thing that defuses it: the re-score
never used the labels. It is a deterministic rule over the package files,
blind tree IDs in, hits out. The honest criticism is not bias - it is that
this was a natural check I should have specified up front and run during the
blinded review. I did not think of it until the rule was shown to be wrong.

DON'T say "with the labels known" as if the labels fed into the scoring. They
did not. Say "after unblinding, but label-blind by construction".

DON'T: call this a skill-file win. It is post-hoc, one criterion, n = 9-20, no test.

IF ASKED about post-unblinding: my original detector only matched set.seed(<literal>)
and scored zero hits on the starting package itself; I fixed the rule after
unblinding. The re-score is a pure function of the package files with no access to
arm labels, so the timing cannot bias the direction. Full three-way table in backup.
:::

## The part I did not expect {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.4em;"}
My primary measure, the AI judge, had **12 criteria**. Ten never fired.
:::

::: {.fragment style="font-size:1.15em; margin-top:.7em;"}
Our maintainer email, **unchanged in all 57 runs**:<br>
fine **10** times, a problem **47** times.
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.9em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700; text-align:center; font-size:1.15em;"}
Every "finding" was my instrument. Not my arms.
:::

::: notes
SAY: "Same text, opposite verdicts. I only saw it by reading the judge's own
justifications - the counts looked like a clean signal."

CHECKPOINT: arrive here by 6:15. Late? Say only the SAY line on this and the next slide.

DON'T: generalise to all LLM judges - one package, one rubric, one rep per tree.

IF ASKED "is the experiment void?": no. The machine-check result came from R CMD check
and stands. What's void is the idea that the judge added sensitivity - and it was the
pre-registered primary, so on what a human reviewer would object to I have no working
endpoint.
IF ASKED about the other criterion that fired: one sentence in the starting package,
flagged in 23 trees, excused in 2, file never opened in 29 (3 n/a).
:::

## What I am *not* claiming

- **Not** "skill files are useless": this is the machine-checkable part of CRAN prep,
  with the docs at hand
- **N = 1**: one package, one agent model, a judge from the **same vendor**. Not powered;
  n was set by budget
- **A protocol deviation**: one arm's file never reached the model. Those 10 runs
  joined the control

::: notes
SAY the three bullets quickly. Credibility is the currency of a null result.

IF ASKED about the deviation: the hindsight arm ran ten times with no file. Its first
API call was 7,145 tokens in every run - identical to the control - while every real
skill arm was larger. Caught afterwards from that token count; pooled on that
evidence, not on outcomes (LESSONS_LEARNED.md section 0).
IF ASKED about the model: Claude Opus 5.5 in Claude Code; judge Claude Sonnet 5.
IF ASKED about n: planned 5 per arm; after an unblinded look we extended to 10 because
budget allowed, not to chase a result. Counts are descriptive, no tests, so there is
no error rate to inflate. Never call it an interim analysis or a pre-registered n=10.
IF ASKED about lost runs: 3 died on API rate limits (two at 1 turn, $0.00), so
`r n_runs` of 60 analysed; excluded, not rerun - a run replayed weeks later is not the
same experimental unit.
:::

## Take home {background-color="#161616" style="color:#FCFCFC"}

::: {style="font-size:1.1em; line-height:1.5;"}
::: {.fragment}
**1.** Effects that change over time hide in averages → `orthoMTL`
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.4em;"}
**2.** Agents do well what a **machine** can check. Invest in **executable checks** first.
:::
::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.4em;"}
**3.** I set out to measure skill files. My judge **measured itself**.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment style="margin-top:.6em; text-align:center; font-size:1.2em; color:#FF4E00; font-weight:700;"}
Machine checks are cheap. Judgement isn't.
:::

::: notes
SAY: three clicks, one sentence each, then the closing line - slowly. Stop talking.

Earlier closing line, if preferred: "Generation got cheap. Verification did not."
:::

[`github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL`](https://github.com/Novartis/orthoMTL) · Vervier et al. 2014 · Juric et al. 2026 · full references in backup
:::

| Checklist | `cran-extrachecks` | [posit-dev/skills](https://github.com/posit-dev/skills) | 9 | A1 |
| Process | `cran-submit` | [CoryMcCartan/agent-skills](https://github.com/CoryMcCartan/agent-skills) | 9 | A2 |
| General R | `r-package-development` | [posit-dev/skills](https://github.com/posit-dev/skills) | 10 | A3 |
| Handbook | raw handbook text | CRAN docs, next slide | 9 | A5 |

Every arm, **the control included**, also had the same offline CRAN docs on disk.
57 of 60 planned runs completed; 3 ended on API rate limits.

Agent: Claude Opus 5.5 (`claude-opus-5-5`) in Claude Code 2.1.282–284 (auto-updated mid-experiment).
Judge: Claude Sonnet 5, same vendor family as the agent. Skill files were delivered as an
always-loaded `CLAUDE.md`, not through the on-demand Skill tool, which the agent did not have.
The control has 20 runs because a second batch of 10 (repo code A4) was meant to carry a hindsight
file written from the rejection history and never received it: first-call context was 7,145 tokens
in all 10, identical to the control. They are pooled with the control. A later paired run with the file delivered is on
the last backup slide.

## Backup: the handbook every arm could read {.smaller}

Snapshot captured **2026-09-18**, identical across all 60 runs.

| Source | URL |
|:--|:--|
| CRAN Cookbook | [contributor.r-project.org/cran-cookbook](https://contributor.r-project.org/cran-cookbook/) |
| CRAN Repository Policy | [cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/policies.html) |
| CRAN Submission Checklist | [cran.r-project.org/web/packages/submission_checklist.html](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/submission_checklist.html) |

The Cookbook is built from real CRAN re-submissions and co-authored by a member
of the CRAN team: the closest public thing to the reviewers' own knowledge.
The handbook arm loaded this text directly into context; the other arms were told where it was.

::: notes
This is the HANDBOOK/COMMUNITY provenance boundary: a criterion derivable from
these three documents is HANDBOOK, anything else is COMMUNITY.
If asked why the control is not "no information at all": because that is not the
realistic alternative. The real alternative is a competent person with the docs.
In trial terms this is an add-on design against an ACTIVE control (standard of
care), not placebo. Pre-specified, and conservative by design.
:::

## Backup: the hedges, in their own words {.smaller}

| Finding | Source |
|:--|:--|
| Skills "often provide no benefit, and can even hurt performance while incurring additional token costs" | SkillDelta, Xu et al. 2026 |
| Human-authored skills +16.2 pp; **LLM-authored skills give no measurable gain** | SkillAxe, Gautam et al. 2026 |
| Agents used retrieved skills 70% of the time yet showed **no performance gain** where the corpus lacked good skills for the domain | SkillFlow, Li et al. 2026 |
| Self-generated skills landed **below** the no-skills baseline (−8 to −11.5 pp) | SkillsBench, Li et al. 2026 |

My null is the same shape, in a domain none of them covered.

## Backup: the counterweight {.smaller}

The headline positive result is **SkillsBench**: curated skills lift pass rate
33.9% → 50.5% (**+16.6 pp**) across 87 tasks and 18 model–harness configurations.
I am not disputing it. Three things make it a different question from mine:

- **8 domains**: natural science, media, cybersecurity, industrial, finance, office, software engineering, maths/OR. **No R, no packaging, no CRAN**
- Tasks are admitted only if **"significantly easier with Skills"**; no-separation tasks are rejected as low-signal
- Skills are drawn from the **top quality quartile** (10.1/12 vs ecosystem mean 6.2/12); the authors call this "an optimistic scenario"

Their own domain gradient points my way: **software engineering +11.6 pp**,
second-lowest of eight, against natural science **+28.8 pp**, "domains with
stronger pretraining and tooling coverage benefit less."

::: notes
Use this slide only if challenged. The honest summary: SkillsBench asks "how much
can a good skill help where a skill should help?" I ask "did a skill help on the
job I actually had?" My four defects were not chosen for skill-dependence, and
three of four are machine-detectable. The two results bracket the same effect
from opposite ends rather than conflicting.
:::

## Backup: the three ways we checked correctness {.smaller}

| Check | What it proves |
|:--|:--|
| Against the old validated package | identical coefficients on 5 fixed cases |
| Flip every label | answer must flip; `0.62` → `0.000` |
| Simulated data, known truth | recovers the right features, 10/10 seeds |

::: notes
The survival path is exactly where comparing against the old code cannot reach —
there was no old survival code. That is why the simulation oracle exists.
:::

## Backup: our own maintainer address {.smaller}

Even a noisy judge can be right once. It flagged our own maintainer address in
47 of 57 trees: `kevin.vervier@novartis.com`

CRAN requires **a person, not a mailing list**, kept current and reachable
"**without any form of filtering**". A corporate account is one re-org away
from failing all three. **Not a violation today. Changing in 0.2.0 anyway.**

::: notes
Tell only if there is time in Q&A, and tell it precisely or someone will correct me.

It is NOT currently against the rules - a named person at a company address is
compliant. The exposure is filtering and job changes, both anticipated by the
policy language. Say "not a violation today" out loud; do not oversell it.

Do NOT say "a newer model spotted this". It is criterion C13, it was in the
corpus from the start. A broken instrument can still be right once; that is not
evidence it works.

No arm ever changed the address - it is still the same in all 57 runs. The 10
COMPLIANT verdicts (7 of them in the handbook arm) are the judge excusing the
corporate domain because Novartis Pharma AG is also the listed copyright holder.
That is judge variance on an under-specified criterion, not an arm fixing anything.
:::

## Backup: what I would change {.smaller}

- Score **R01 (`set.seed()`)** with a rule that also sees seeds passed as default arguments
- Plant more defects only a **CRAN volunteer** could catch, and calibrate the judge on them
- A **positive control** in the blinded run, plus a pre-flight check that each arm's file reaches the model
- A **handicapped arm** with the CRAN docs removed: if it does worse, the measurement has teeth
- Judge each package several times, not once
- More packages, more models

## Backup: the four planted defects {.smaller}

| Defect | Caught by `R CMD check`? | Repaired |
|:--|:--|:--|
| `NAMESPACE` deleted | yes, check cannot even run | 57/57 |
| `usethis` LICENSE template vs GPL-3 DESCRIPTION | **no**, this is rejection **R02** | **57/57** |
| DESCRIPTION metadata (`Authors@R`, title case) | yes | 57/57 |
| Unused declared `Imports` | yes | 57/57 |

Three of four are machine-visible. Our other real rejection, **R01, the
hard-coded `set.seed()`**, was left in the starting package as a fifth defect that
`R CMD check` does not report; it is on the next slide.

Three of four machine-visible is the result's main caveat: this measures the
easy half of CRAN preparation.

## Backup: the hard-coded seed (R01) {.smaller}

| Arm | n | Canonical fix (`seed = NULL`) | Default kept, RNG restored | Still hard-coded |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Control | 20 | 0 | 10 | 10 |
| Checklist | 9 | 0 | 8 | 1 |
| Process | 9 | 7 | 1 | 1 |
| General R | 10 | 0 | 7 | 3 |
| Handbook | 9 | 8 | 0 | 1 |

Completed runs; descriptive, no test. "Default kept": `seed = 42` stays but a helper restores the
user's RNG state: arguably acceptable, not what the reviewer asked for. Control includes the 10
runs whose hindsight file never arrived.

**Re-scored after unblinding.** The original rule only matched `set.seed(<literal>)`, so it scored
**zero hits on the starting package itself**. The fixed rule reads package files only and never
touches the blind map: the same code at first unblinding gives this same table.

::: notes
Be upfront - I planted what I could verify automatically, which is exactly the
half where the control was always going to do well. The honest version of this
experiment seeds the other half, and that is the first thing I would change.

On the post-unblinding point, say it before anyone asks, and say it in this order:
(1) the rule was wrong, (2) here is how it was wrong, (3) it is a pure function of
tree content, so the timing cannot have biased the direction. rescore_r01.R takes
a tree path and returns hits; it has no access to arm labels. Validated on 8
synthetic cases, the starting package (3 hits), baseline and control (0), and a mutant (1).

The fair criticism is NOT that the labels contaminated the scoring - they were
never an input. It is that this was an obvious check to specify up front and
run inside the blinded review, and I only thought of it once the original rule
was shown to miss the very defect it was written for. Concede that version
plainly; it is a design oversight, not a bias.

I am NOT claiming this as a skill-file win. Two things block that. It is one
criterion at n=9-10 with no test, and it is a post-hoc re-score. The controls
(n=20, including the 10 runs that never got the hindsight file) produced the canonical fix zero times in 20 runs, which
makes the process/handbook contrast more interesting, not proven. Report it as the most
interesting loose end in the dataset and move on.

If asked why the process and handbook arms and nobody else: the cookbook contains the canonical
seed = NULL pattern verbatim, in a section every arm could read. The handbook arm had that text
front-loaded into context rather than pointed at; the process skill is the adversarial-review
arm. That is a hypothesis about front-loading vs distillation, not a finding.
:::

## Backup: positive control, run afterwards (R01) {.smaller}

The hindsight file was written from CRAN's own two rejection messages, installed, and checked to
reach the model (first-call context +1,055 tokens over its paired control). Then a fresh control and the
hindsight arm were run as 10 interleaved pairs, **after unblinding, labels known**, on a newer
Claude Code (2.1.294).

| Arm | n | Canonical fix (`seed = NULL`) | Default kept | Still hard-coded |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Fresh control | 10 | 0 | 6 | 4 |
| Hindsight file delivered | 10 | 10 | 0 | 0 |

Two extra hindsight runs without a surviving partner (rate limits) were also canonical: 12 of 12.
This is a ceiling check, not a skill-file result: the file contains the answer. It shows the
seed defect is learnable from text in context, which the blinded experiment could not show. Not
pooled with the 57; no judge panel was run on these trees. `R CMD check` was identical across
arms: no errors or warnings in any of the 22 trees. Scripts and scores: `supplementary/`.

::: notes
Frame as an afterward positive control. Do NOT say the blinded experiment would have given the
same result: different CLI version, labels known, no judge. The claim is only that when the file
is delivered, the instrument sees the fix.
:::
